extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy and natural philosophy (metaphysics, etiology, philosophy of science)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of the relation between etiology (scientific causal explanation) and metaphysical 'forces' (the will/Ideas), prescribing what scientific explanation must and must not do when treating natural phenomena and organisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Etiology's primary task
rubrics_metrics.description: Etiology must seek out the causes of all phenomena in nature, i.e., the circumstances under which they invariably appear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It must refer the multitude of phenomena which have various forms in various circumstances to what is active in every phenomenon and is presupposed in the cause—original forces of nature. ('It must seek out the causes of all phenomena in nature, _i.e._, the circumstances under which they invariably appear.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Refer phenomena to underlying forces
rubrics_metrics.description: Refer varied manifestations to the original forces of nature that are active in every phenomenon and presupposed in the causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Etiology should identify the universal force(s) underlying particular causal chains, treating those forces as the presupposition of causal explanation rather than replacing causal explanation with metaphysical claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish force-difference from circumstance-difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Correctly distinguish between a difference of the phenomenon which arises from a difference of the force, and one which results merely from a difference of the circumstances under which the force expresses itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guard against prematurely positing new forces for what are merely different expressions of the same force under varying conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conflating distinct forces or splitting one force
rubrics_metrics.description: Guard against taking the expressions of one and the same force under different circumstances for the manifestations of different forces, and conversely against taking for manifestations of one and the same force what originally belongs to different forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the faculty of judgment to avoid both over-splitting and over-unifying—this is why few can advance physics despite many enlarging experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physics must enumerate and characterize universal forces
rubrics_metrics.description: Physics should accurately define, enumerate, and distinguish the universal forces which are active in causes and effects, and then indicate all the different effects in which each force appears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When physics has accomplished this thoroughly in every particular, 'There will then remain no unknown force in unorganised nature, nor any effect, which has not been proved to be the manifestation of one of these forces under definite circumstances, in accordance with a law of nature.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a law of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: A law of nature is the relation of the Idea to the form of its manifestation; more practically, it is the observed rule according to which nature invariably proceeds when definite circumstances occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A law of nature 'may be defined as a fact expressed generally—_un fait généralisé_'; a complete enumeration of laws would be a complete register of facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Morphology's descriptive role
rubrics_metrics.description: Morphology completes consideration of nature as a whole by enumerating, comparing, and arranging all the enduring forms of organised nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Morphology has little to say of causes of individual appearance (procreation/generatio æquivoca), but is the inventory and comparison of enduring forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of causal (etiological) explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Causal explanation applies to particular phenomena in time and space but cannot reach the inner reality (the will or 'thing-in-itself'), which lies outside the principle of sufficient reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every movement must have a cause insofar as it is a particular phenomenon; but the universal common nature (original forces) remains a 'qualitas occulta' where etiological explanation ends and metaphysical inquiry begins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid premature appeal to original forces
rubrics_metrics.description: Indolence and ignorance make us disposed to appeal too soon to original forces; do not use them where causal/etiological explanation suffices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text warns against the scholastic habit of invoking quidities and entities too readily; physics demands causes operating in time and space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reduction of higher grades to lower ones
rubrics_metrics.description: It is an error for natural science to seek to refer the higher grades of the objectification of will (e.g., organisms, life) to the lower (physical, chemical, mechanical) forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reduce physiological functions or organismal form to mere 'form and combination' of physical forces; such reductionism confuses form with inner content and is criticized (e.g., Descartes, Lamarck, mechanistic physiologists).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not force monistic reduction to one known force
rubrics_metrics.description: Etiology should not abandon its province by trying to deny all original forces except perhaps one (e.g., impenetrability) and forcefully refer all others to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a method supplants content by form and would ultimately yield error instead of truth—physics must acknowledge distinct original forces when warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original forces are groundless and lie outside causality
rubrics_metrics.description: Original forces (the will at a grade of objectification) are 'groundless'—they lie outside the chain of causes and effects and the principle of sufficient reason, being the 'immediate objectivity of will'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When explaining phenomena etiologically, one reaches a 'qualitas occulta' where metaphysics begins; do not mistake this for a causal first link to which causal chains can be entirely reduced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Etiology and philosophy are complementary but distinct
rubrics_metrics.description: Etiology (science) deals with causes in time and space and practical application; philosophy concerns itself with the universal, the original forces, and the will as 'thing-in-itself'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep their aims and methods distinct: etiology supplies instances and causal conditions; philosophy treats the inner nature and grades of objectification of will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search for analogies and fundamental types, but avoid species-mixing
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognise the unity of will reflected as analogies across phenomena (e.g., polarity, analogy between crystallisation and ossification), which justifies seeking fundamental types and family likenesses in morphology and comparative anatomy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use analogies to guide systematisation (l’unité de plan) but do not conflate species or explain higher forms as mere variations of lower ones; analogies indicate relation, not identity of species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of lower-grade forces within higher phenomena (permitted but limited)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although higher grades (organisms) are not reducible to lower forces, the vital force 'avails itself of and uses the forces of unorganised nature'—physical and chemical forces operate within limits in organisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept application of physical/chemical explanation where appropriate and bounded, but reject wholesale reduction of life and organismal form to those forces alone ('the hammer and anvil' analogy).
